Without a user mapping, sub becomes the user ID, preferred_username the username, name the display name and picture the avatar, and phone_number fills the phone. The Casdoor sign-in page recognizes a custom provider whose auth URL points at oauth.telegram.org and keeps the OAuth state short for it.

Note that a Telegram user signed in through the widget and the same person signed in through OIDC are not automatically the same Casdoor user. The widget identity is the numeric id, while the OIDC identity is sub, and Telegram's own examples show different values for the two. Pick one method per application.

X (Twitter) and Facebook​

These two are ordinary OAuth 2.0, but each has a detail worth knowing.

X requires a PKCE challenge on its OAuth 2.0 authorize URL. Casdoor's Twitter type generates a new code verifier for every sign-in, sends the S256 challenge, and passes the verifier in the token exchange, so there is nothing to configure beyond the client ID and secret. Casdoor requests the users.read tweet.read scopes and reads the user from /2/users/me, which gives the user ID, the handle and the display name. It doesn't request an email field, so plan for X users without an email address. The Twitter provider guide covers the app settings.

Facebook returns an app-scoped user ID: the same person has a different ID in each Facebook app, so moving to a new Facebook app means your users won't match their old records unless you link them by email. Casdoor asks for email,public_profile and reads id, name, picture and email from the Graph API. Facebook omits email when the profile has no valid address. See the Facebook provider guide.

How your app sees all of this: plain OIDC​

Your application never talks to Steam, Telegram, X or Facebook. It is an OIDC client of Casdoor, configured once with the Casdoor issuer, https://<your-casdoor-host>/.well-known/openid-configuration. You add the social providers to the Casdoor application on its Providers tab, and their buttons appear on the Casdoor sign-in page.

After any of these sign-ins, Casdoor finds or creates a Casdoor user and finishes the normal authorization code flow with your app. The ID token your app receives is signed by Casdoor, and its sub is the Casdoor user ID, not the SteamID or the Telegram ID. So your app needs no OpenID 2.0 library, no HMAC code, no PKCE quirks per provider, and no special case for users without an email. The original provider ID is stored on the Casdoor user, for example in the steam or telegram field, if you ever need it.

A few things to plan for:

  • Account linking. Casdoor links a social sign-in to an existing user by verified email, verified phone, or username, in the order the application's binding rule sets. Steam and widget-based Telegram provide neither email nor phone, so they create a separate user unless the user links the provider from an account that is already signed in. See how Casdoor links accounts.
  • Extra profile fields. Providers that pass on raw data, such as the Goth-based Steam type and custom providers, can fill more user fields through user mapping.
  • The client side. Any standard library works against Casdoor. Connect a standard OIDC client lists the endpoints, and the Spring Boot SSO with OIDC post shows a complete app.

References​

  • Steam Web API and OpenID: steamcommunity.com/dev
  • Steamworks, User Authentication and Ownership: partner.steamgames.com/doc/features/auth
  • Telegram, Log In With Telegram (OpenID Connect): core.telegram.org/bots/telegram-login
  • Telegram, Login Widget (legacy): core.telegram.org/widgets/login-legacy
  • X, OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow with PKCE: docs.x.com
  • Meta, Graph API User reference: developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/reference/user
  • Casdoor source: idp/telegram.go, idp/goth.go, idp/custom.go

item.title: Dummy Payment Gateway for Testing: Casdoor's Dummy Provider, Stripe Test Mode and PayPal Sandbox
item.description: A dummy payment gateway completes checkout without moving money. How the Casdoor Dummy provider works, and when to switch to Stripe test mode or PayPal sandbox.
item.content:encoded:
A dummy payment gateway is a payment provider that accepts every checkout as paid without contacting a bank or card network, so you can test orders, subscriptions and fulfillment with no money and no gateway account. Casdoor ships one: the Dummy payment provider. Add it to a product, buy the product, and Casdoor records the payment and the order as Paid, starts the subscription and writes the transaction, all without leaving your server. Use Dummy in development, and switch to a vendor sandbox (Stripe test mode, PayPal sandbox, Paddle sandbox) in staging, where you also need declined cards, 3-D Secure and real redirects.

Dummy, Balance and vendor sandboxes at a glance​

ProviderTest environmentHow Casdoor picks test or liveCasdoor provider type
DummyNone needed, every payment succeedsAlways simulatedDummy
BalanceInternal, funded by a recharge productAlways internalBalance
StripeSandbox with sk_test_ / pk_test_ keysBy the keys you enterStripe
PayPalSandbox apps and sandbox accountsrunmode other than prod uses the sandboxPayPal
PaddleSeparate sandbox account at sandbox-vendors.paddle.comrunmode other than prod uses sandbox-api.paddle.comPaddle
AdyenTest environment (checkout-test.adyen.com)runmode other than prod uses the test environmentAdyen
AirWallexSeparate sandbox accountrunmode other than prod calls api-demo.airwallex.comAirWallex
Lemon SqueezyStore test mode with test-mode API keysBy the API key you enterLemon Squeezy
FastSpringTest storefront with .test. in the hostBy the Host you enterFastSpring
PolarSandbox at sandbox.polar.shNot supported, Casdoor always calls api.polar.shPolar

runmode is the option in conf/app.conf (or the runmode environment variable) described in the configuration reference. Its default is dev, so a fresh Casdoor talks to the sandboxes of PayPal, Paddle, Adyen and AirWallex until you set it to prod.

What a dummy transaction means​

A dummy transaction runs through the same records as a real purchase (order, payment, subscription, ledger entry) but moves no money. It is different from a sandbox transaction. A sandbox still calls the vendor's API, shows the vendor's checkout page and sends webhooks; only the money is fake. A dummy transaction never leaves your system.

That difference decides what each one can test. A dummy gateway is good for your own logic: does the plan grant the right role, does the order show up, does the coupon count as used, does the user land on the right page. A sandbox is good for the integration: credentials, redirects, card declines, authentication challenges and webhook delivery. You need both, at different stages.

How the Casdoor Dummy provider works​

The Dummy provider has no settings and no payment page. Here is the full flow on Casdoor master:

  1. When the user pays, the provider's Pay call returns the Casdoor result page as the payment URL. It packs the price and currency into the order ID instead of creating anything at a vendor.
  2. Casdoor stores the payment in state Created and sends the browser straight to the result page. There is no card form, fake or otherwise.
  3. The result page sees a Created payment and calls POST /api/notify-payment about a second later.
  4. The provider's Notify call always answers Paid, with the price it packed earlier, so the price check passes.
  5. Casdoor then runs the normal success path: the payment and the order become Paid, the subscriptions created for the payment are updated, a Purchase transaction is written, product stock is reduced and a coupon on the order is marked as used. If the product is a recharge product, a Recharge transaction also adds the amount to the user's balance.

So yes, Dummy marks the order as paid right away, and the user sees the success page with no step in between.

Two limits follow from that design. Dummy can't fail: there is no way to make it return Canceled, Timeout or Error, so failure paths need a sandbox. And Dummy can't renew: Casdoor only allows auto renewal for Balance and Stripe, so a subscription bought with Dummy always has auto renewal off.

On a new database, Casdoor creates a built-in Dummy provider named provider_payment_dummy in the admin organization, next to a built-in Balance provider. You can also add your own: in Identity > Providers, set Category to Payment and Type to Dummy.

Keep Dummy out of production​

/api/notify-payment is open to anonymous callers, because real gateways call it without a Casdoor session. For a real provider that is safe, since Notify checks the payment with the vendor. Dummy checks nothing and reports Paid. Any product that lists Dummy in its Payment providers shows it at checkout, and anyone who picks it gets the product for free. Remove Dummy from every product before you go live, and do not put it on products in an organization that real users can reach.

Balance: the internal wallet you can fund with Dummy​

The Balance provider lets users pay from their account balance. Casdoor checks the balance first, deducts the price, and marks the payment and order Paid in the same request. Balance is a real production feature, not a test tool, but it pairs well with Dummy: put Dummy on a recharge product, "top up" a test user, and the balance is credited with no money involved.

This matters for subscriptions, because Balance is one of the two providers that support auto renewal. With Dummy plus Balance you can test the whole renewal loop on a laptop with no gateway account.

Vendor sandboxes for staging​

Stripe. Stripe separates test and live data by keys: sandbox keys start with pk_test_ and sk_test_, live keys with pk_live_ and sk_live_, and objects in one mode are not visible in the other. Casdoor uses whatever keys you put in the Stripe provider; runmode does not change anything for Stripe. Stripe's test cards cover the paths Dummy can't: 4242 4242 4242 4242 succeeds, 4000 0000 0000 0002 is declined, and 4000 0000 0000 3220 requires 3-D Secure. Use any future expiry and any CVC. Stripe's terms forbid testing in live mode with real card details.

PayPal. The PayPal sandbox is a separate environment with its own apps and test accounts. PayPal creates a default personal and a default business sandbox account when you first sign in to the developer dashboard; you pay with the personal one. Create the app in sandbox mode, put its credentials in the PayPal provider, and keep runmode at dev.

Paddle. The sandbox is a separate account at sandbox-vendors.paddle.com with its own keys and products; nothing is shared with live. Paddle's test cards include 4242 4242 4242 4242 (succeeds) and 4000 0000 0000 0002 (declined).

Lemon Squeezy has a test mode per store, and API keys created in test mode only see test data. FastSpring test orders go through a test storefront: insert .test. into the store host, for example yourstore.test.onfastspring.com, and enter that as the provider's Host. Polar has a sandbox with its own tokens, but the Casdoor Polar provider does not select it, so a Polar provider in Casdoor always works against live Polar. Alipay in Casdoor is also hard-wired to production.

A test plan for Casdoor products, plans and subscriptions​

Development, with Dummy​

  1. Create a product and add Dummy to its Payment providers.
  2. Create a plan for that product and a pricing page that lists it (see the pricing overview).
  3. As a test user, open the pricing page and buy the plan. Check that the payment and the order are Paid, the subscription is Active, and a Purchase transaction appears on the user.
  4. Sign in as the user and check that the plan's role took effect in your application.
  5. If the plan has Is exclusive on, buy it again and expect the error that the user already has an active subscription.
  6. Apply a coupon at checkout and check that its usage is recorded.
  7. Create a recharge product with Dummy, top up the test user, then buy the plan with Balance and Auto renew on.
  8. To test renewal without waiting a month, edit the subscription's End time on its edit page so it ends within 24 hours. Casdoor checks subscriptions once an hour; expect Renewal state Renewed and a new subscription for the next period. Then buy the plan again with a balance too low for the next period, move its end time the same way, and expect Failed with the reason in Renewal message. The subscription docs describe the exact rules.

Staging, with a sandbox​

  1. Run staging with runmode = dev and sandbox or test credentials only.
  2. Replace Dummy with the provider you will use in production, configured with its sandbox keys.
  3. Repeat the purchase and check that the browser goes to the vendor's checkout and comes back to the Casdoor result page.
  4. With Stripe, pay once with the decline card and once with the 3-D Secure card, and check the payment and order states for each.
  5. With Stripe and Auto renew on, Casdoor saves the card at checkout and charges it itself at renewal, so the end-time trick above works in the sandbox too.

Going live​

Remove Dummy from all products, set runmode = prod if you use PayPal, Paddle, Adyen or AirWallex, and swap in live keys. Check the payment records of the first real orders.

If you also test sign-up email in the same environment, a local mail catcher keeps those messages off real inboxes; see MailHog vs Mailpit.

References​

  • Casdoor source: pp/dummy.go, pp/balance.go, object/order_pay.go, object/payment.go, object/subscription_renew.go
  • Casdoor docs: Payment providers, Dummy, Balance, Subscription
  • Stripe: Testing, API keys
  • PayPal: Sandbox, Sandbox accounts
  • Paddle: Sandbox
  • Lemon Squeezy: Test mode
  • FastSpring: Test orders
  • Polar: Sandbox
  • Adyen: Live endpoints

item.title: Casdoor v4: A New Console, a Marketplace, and OAuth for MCP Servers
item.description: Casdoor v4.0 came out on September 1. Two months and 25 releases later we are at v4.25, so this is a good point to look back at what changed. In short: the admin console was rebuilt, self-hosting got a lot less fiddly, there is now a Marketplace for integrations and sign-in themes, and Casdoor can act as the authorization server for MCP servers and AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Casdoor v4.0 came out on September 1. Two months and 25 releases later we are at v4.25, so this is a good point to look back at what changed. In short: the admin console was rebuilt, self-hosting got a lot less fiddly, there is now a Marketplace for integrations and sign-in themes, and Casdoor can act as the authorization server for MCP servers and AI agents.

If you haven't used it: Casdoor is an open-source identity and access management platform written in Go. It is a full identity provider, not a library or a login proxy. Users live in Casdoor, Casdoor issues the tokens, and your apps talk to it over OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0, CAS, LDAP or SCIM. Authorization is handled by Apache Casbin, so ACL, RBAC and ABAC models all work. It is Apache-2.0 licensed and listed in the CNCF Landscape.

A rebuilt console and sign-in pages​

v4.0 replaced the Ant Design admin console with a new one built on shadcn/ui, Tailwind and Vite (now on React 19). It has a command palette, bulk row selection, inline form validation, two-column forms and tables where you can hide columns. Switching languages no longer reloads the page.

The sign-in, sign-up and password reset pages were redesigned too. Dark mode works properly, and the pages are usable on a phone.

If you are upgrading from v3, read the upgrade guide linked from the README first. The main thing to check is the path of the frontend build if you serve static files through a CDN or reverse proxy.

Easier to self-host​

A lot of the v4 work came from issues and forum threads by people running Casdoor themselves:

  • No default password. On first visit Casdoor asks you to set the admin password, or you can set it with initAdminPassword.
  • Sub-path deployment. Set basePath to serve Casdoor at https://example.com/auth/ instead of its own host.
  • Forward auth. Casdoor has a forward auth endpoint for Traefik, Caddy and Nginx, so you can put apps that have no login of their own behind it, with public paths and per-site rules.
  • Docker tags. Images are now also tagged X, X.Y and X.Y.Z, so you can follow a major or minor version.
  • Helm. The chart moved into the main repository, is published to GHCR and Artifact Hub with every release, and can hold organizations, applications and users as configuration. See Running Casdoor on Kubernetes.
  • Windows service. The binary can run as a Windows service.
  • Upgrades. The system info page shows the latest release and can upgrade an official binary in one click.
  • Operations. Container health checks, Prometheus counters for sign-in success and failure, audit logs forwarded to Syslog, and Redis Cluster support.

Marketplace​

The new Marketplace lets an admin install integrations from inside Casdoor: application templates, identity providers and sign-in themes. Installing one fills in the configuration for you, and uninstalling restores what was there before.

There are more than 20 sign-in themes so far. You can preview a theme on your own sign-in page before installing it. Organization admins can also customize the sign-in pages with their own fonts, images and HTML, within an allowlist that blocks forms and scripts. The read-only demo at door.casdoor.com cycles through the themes if you want to see them.

OAuth for MCP servers and AI agents​

The MCP specification asks remote MCP servers to use OAuth, and MCP clients usually don't know in advance which authorization server they will meet. Casdoor now covers the pieces this needs:

  • OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow with PKCE, and a consent page where users can grant only some of the requested scopes
  • Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) and client management (RFC 7592)
  • Client ID Metadata Documents: an MCP client can use a URL as its client_id without registering first
  • private_key_jwt client authentication for dynamically registered clients
  • Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) and Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)
  • Token Exchange (RFC 8693), including ID-JAGs for enterprise-managed authorization, so an organization's IdP can decide which agents may reach which MCP servers

Point your MCP server's protected resource metadata at Casdoor, and sign-in, consent, token issuing and validation are handled for you. Casdoor also runs its own MCP server, so an assistant such as Claude Code or Cursor can manage users, applications and permissions through it.

Other protocol work​

  • SAML Single Logout and IdP-initiated SSO
  • OIDC prompt=none, better conformance for hybrid flow, prompt and max_age, and the RFC 9207 iss parameter
  • Token revocation (RFC 7009), DPoP and the device authorization flow
  • Magic link sign-in, password history checks, and passkeys shared across sibling subdomains
  • Exclusive sign-in with a maximum number of sessions per user

Try it​

The quickest way to look around:

docker run -p 8000:8000 casbin/casdoor-all-in-one

Then open http://localhost:8000. The image includes SQLite and sample data, so use it for trying things out, not for production. The installation guide covers real deployments.

There are two online demos: demo.casdoor.com is writable and resets every five minutes, and door.casdoor.com is read-only.

If you would rather not run it yourself, Casdoor Cloud gives you a dedicated, managed instance at a flat price with no per-user fees. New accounts get $10 in credit to try it.

Links​

  • GitHub: https://github.com/casdoor/casdoor
  • Release notes: https://github.com/casdoor/casdoor/releases
  • Docs: https://casdoor.ai/docs/overview
  • Discord: https://discord.gg/5rPsrAzK7S

Bug reports and feature requests are welcome on GitHub. If Casdoor is useful to you, a star helps other people find it.

item.title: Running Casdoor on Kubernetes: Official Helm Chart and Configuration as Code
item.description: Casdoor has an official Helm chart. It lives in the main repository under manifests/casdoor, is published with every Casdoor release to GHCR, and is listed on Artifact Hub. Starting with Casdoor v4.18.0, the chart can also hold your organizations, applications, users and providers as declarative configuration: change them in the values file, run helm upgrade, and the running pods apply the change without a restart.
item.content:encoded:
Casdoor has an official Helm chart. It lives in the main repository under manifests/casdoor, is published with every Casdoor release to GHCR, and is listed on Artifact Hub. Starting with Casdoor v4.18.0, the chart can also hold your organizations, applications, users and providers as declarative configuration: change them in the values file, run helm upgrade, and the running pods apply the change without a restart.

This post walks through a Kubernetes deployment from the first helm install to a setup you can keep in Git.

Install​

You need Helm v3.8+ and a cluster:

helm install casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor

The chart version is the Casdoor version, so --version 4.18.0 installs Casdoor 4.18.0. Without an Ingress or Gateway, the service is only reachable inside the cluster. To try it, forward a port:

kubectl port-forward svc/casdoor 8000:8000

Then open http://localhost:8000. On the first visit, Casdoor asks you to set the password of built-in/admin; then sign in with it. See Sign in to the admin console.

A production setup​

The defaults are meant for a quick try: Casdoor stores its data in SQLite inside the container, so it is lost when the pod is replaced. For a real deployment, put the settings below in a values.yaml file and install with helm install casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor -f values.yaml.

External database​

database:
  driver: postgres # or mysql, cockroachdb
  host: postgres.db.svc.cluster.local
  user: casdoor
  password: change-me
  databaseName: casdoor
  sslMode: require

To keep the database password out of the values file, put the whole app.conf in a Secret and set configFromSecret to its name.

Exposing Casdoor​

The chart supports both a classic Ingress and the Gateway API. With an Ingress controller and cert-manager:

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
  hosts:
    - host: door.example.com
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
  tls:
    - secretName: casdoor-tls
      hosts:
        - door.example.com

With the Gateway API (Istio, Envoy Gateway, Cilium, Kong, NGINX Gateway Fabric and others), attach an HTTPRoute to an existing Gateway:

gatewayApi:
  enabled: true
  parentRefs:
    - name: my-gateway
      namespace: gateway-system
  hostnames:
    - door.example.com

The chart can also create the Gateway itself and add an HTTP to HTTPS redirect, see the Helm guide.

More than one replica​

Casdoor keeps sign-in sessions on local disk by default. Before running more than one replica, point all of them to the same Redis, so a user stays signed in whichever pod serves the request. Every app.conf setting can be passed as an environment variable, so the endpoint can come from a Secret:

replicaCount: 3

envFromSecret:
  - name: redisEndpoint
    secretName: casdoor-redis
    key: endpoint # host:port, or host:port,db,password

The same Redis is used for the OAuth device flow state. Once Redis is in place, autoscaling.enabled: true adds a HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

Configuration as code​

Clicking organizations and applications together in the web UI is fine for a first test, but most teams want the setup of their identity provider reviewed and versioned like the rest of their infrastructure. The initData values do that:

initData:
  enabled: true
  data:
    organizations:
      - owner: admin
        name: acme
        displayName: Acme
        passwordType: bcrypt
    applications:
      - owner: admin
        name: app-acme-portal
        organization: acme
        displayName: Acme Portal
        redirectUris:
          - https://portal.acme.example.com/callback
    users:
      - owner: acme
        name: alice
        displayName: Alice
        password: change-me
        signupApplication: app-acme-portal
    roles:
      - owner: acme
        name: admins
        displayName: Admins
        users: [acme/alice]
        isEnabled: true

The chart stores the data in a Secret and mounts it into the pods. Casdoor applies it at startup, then checks it every 30 seconds (initData.watchInterval). When you change the data and run helm upgrade, kubelet updates the mounted Secret and the running pods apply it without a restart.

A few rules make this safe to use alongside the web UI:

  • Only the fields you write are managed. An object that already exists gets the fields set in the file; its other fields keep the values edited in the UI. You can manage just the redirect URIs of an application, and leave the rest to the admin console.
  • Passwords are initial passwords. A user's password is only used when the user is created, so users can change theirs afterwards.
  • Nothing is deleted. Removing an object from the file doesn't remove it from Casdoor.
  • Errors don't take Casdoor down. If an object fails to apply, the error is logged and Casdoor keeps serving; the data is retried on every check until it applies.

The file format is the one Casdoor has always used for data initialization: organizations, applications, users, providers, certs, roles, permissions, groups, LDAP servers, webhooks, plans, pricings and more, with the same field names as the REST API. A quick way to get started is to export an existing instance with casdoor -export and keep the objects you want to manage.

To keep the data out of the values file, for example when it is managed by Sealed Secrets or External Secrets, create the Secret yourself:

initData:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: casdoor-init-data
  existingSecretKey: init_data.yaml

The same feature works without Kubernetes. Mount a JSON or YAML file and set:

initDataFile = /init-data/init_data.yaml
initDataMerge = true
initDataWatchInterval = 30

Or use Terraform​

If you prefer terraform plan, imports of existing objects and drift detection, the official Terraform provider manages the same objects through the Casdoor API:

resource "casdoor_application" "portal" {
  name          = "app-acme-portal"
  organization  = "acme"
  redirect_uris = ["https://portal.acme.example.com/callback"]
}

Use the Helm values when the configuration should ship with the deployment, and Terraform when Casdoor is one of many systems you already manage with it. See the Terraform guide.

Coming from the old chart​

Up to v4.15.0, the chart was published as oci://registry-1.docker.io/casbin/casdoor-helm-charts, and the separate casdoor/casdoor-helm repository is now archived. The Docker Hub chart still receives every release, but new installs should use the GHCR one. Moving an existing release over is a regular upgrade, and resource names stay the same:

helm upgrade casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor --version <version>

Links​

  • Helm chart: Artifact Hub · source
  • Guides: Try with Helm · Data initialization and configuration as code · Terraform
  • Don't want to run it yourself? Casdoor Cloud gives you a dedicated Casdoor instance that we host and keep upgraded for you.

On February 22, 2026, Casdoor joined the CNCF Cloud Native Landscape, under the Security & Compliance category in Provisioning. The Landscape brings together widely used cloud-native projects and products; inclusion helps users and enterprises discover and evaluate solutions for building cloud-native systems.

https://landscape.cncf.io/?item=provisioning--security-compliance--casdoor

Casdoor on the CNCF Cloud Native Landscape (Security & Compliance)

About Casdoor​

Casdoor is an open-source, UI-first Identity and Access Management (IAM) / Single Sign-On (SSO) platform with a web UI. It supports OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML, and CAS, as well as many social logins (Google, GitHub, WeChat, etc.), and helps you build user management and SSO in a few steps. Casdoor is developed by Casbin in Golang and React. It uses a front-end/back-end separation architecture, supports high concurrency, and is actively maintained by the community. The project has received over 13k GitHub stars.

About CNCF and the Cloud Native Landscape​

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) is a Linux Foundation project that promotes cloud-native technologies. Its vision is to make cloud native ubiquitous. CNCF maintains the Cloud Native Landscape (https://landscape.cncf.io), which classifies and tracks projects and products in the cloud-native ecosystem and serves as a reference map for developers and enterprises.

Looking ahead​

Joining the CNCF Landscape reflects progress in Casdoor’s maturity and community. We will keep improving Casdoor and its integration with cloud-native workflows, and we welcome more users and contributors to join the community.

Casdoor's SSO simplifies the login process by allowing users to authenticate just once to access multiple services. item.content:encoded:
In an era where digital identity management is crucial, Single Sign-On (SSO) solutions like Casdoor are revolutionizing the way users interact with multiple applications. Casdoor's SSO simplifies the login process by allowing users to authenticate just once to access multiple services. This not only enhances user convenience but also boosts engagement and satisfaction.

For businesses, Casdoor's SSO streamlines user credential management, enhancing security and simplifying new user onboarding. It counters the risk associated with weak or recycled passwords by centralizing user management.

However, in the face of growing online threats, integrating robust security measures in SSO systems like Casdoor is vital. This is where face authentication technology comes into play, adding an extra layer of protection while maintaining user-friendly interactions.

Face authentication employs unique facial characteristics to confirm user identities. It compares live images with stored facial templates, offering a secure yet straightforward way to authenticate users. This method boasts high accuracy, even under varied conditions, and is widely adopted in modern consumer devices.

Integrating face authentication into Casdoor's SSO system promises a secure, efficient, and seamless user experience. To ensure optimal performance, it is crucial to focus on:

  1. Anti-Spoofing Measures: Implementing liveness detection, like tracking eye movements or random gestures, is essential to counteract spoofing attempts and maintain system integrity.

  2. Regular Updates for Improved Accuracy: Keeping the face authentication technology updated with the latest AI and biometric advancements ensures accuracy and enhances user experience. It's vital to use diverse datasets for algorithm training to prevent biases.

  3. Balancing Security and Convenience: The best systems strike a perfect balance between stringent security measures and user convenience. This approach encourages user adoption by ensuring a straightforward authentication process without compromising security.

In conclusion, by integrating face authentication with Casdoor's SSO, businesses can offer a secure, efficient, and user-friendly login experience. This not only fortifies security but also aligns with modern user expectations in the digital world.
